Fabrizio Terzi Home About Work Contact About Testimonials Resume Projects Gallery Hi ! I am Fabrizio Terzi Freelance Researcher, Bergamo Hub e-Learning Specialist Talented Illustrator Good man :) Let's Start Build with love by... terzi.fabrizio@protonmail.com Bergamo Hub (Italy) About Me I build learning ecosystems and help others do the same. For years, I've been active in global online communities, especially around peer-to-peer education and social innovation design. I believe in collaborative learning, open knowledge, and critical infrastructures for shared intelligence. I'm not just a team player—I like to co-design visions that become real. I work well in distributed, self-organizing contexts where purpose and care matter more than hierarchy. Right now, I’m based in Bergamo (Italy) and I co-founded Pyragogy.org , an open-source initiative to reimagine education as a participatory, AI-supported village. We work on rhythm-based learning systems, co-authored publications, and micro-tools for self-education and collaboration. I’ve worked across five continents. I’ve learned that context is everything, and curiosity is not optional. When I’m offline, I try to be somewhere beautiful, with people I care about. Learn. I'm a passionate about Digital Art, Technology and Peer-to-Peer education. I always enjoy "learning by doing" with peers and Its my goal to offer outstanding service to my client needs and project base collaborators. Share. I believes in a bright future and sharing knowledge and our ability to build it together. I collaborate with several global on-line community in order to create a tools and resources to inspire others and help build the world we imagine. Inspire. We can handle projects completely, from an idea and design concept to finished product, get in touch to discuss your project! #Learning City Point The Peeragogy Handbook 2012 - 2015 Project Member Peeragogy team The Peeragogy project seeks to empower the worldwide population of self-motivated learners who use digital media to connect with each other, to co-construct knowledge, to co-learn. Co-learning is ancient; the capacity for learning by imitation and more, to teach others what we know, is the essence of human culture. We are human because we learn together. Today, however, the advent of digital production media and distribution and communication networks has raised the power and potential of co-learning to a new level. If you want to learn how to fix a pipe, solve a partial differential equation, write software, you are seconds away from know-how via YouTube, Wikipedia and search engines. Access to technology and access to knowledge, however, isn't enough. Learning is a social, active, and ongoing process. Title: Untitled

STATUS: ACTIVE /✵Seeding Name: Learning City Point: Problem: To be effective, educational technologies must be designed based on what we know about how people learn. Through interviews with experts in the field, this course explores educational technologies, outlines the theories that influence their development, and examines their use. MIT Course Wrap: A project contributor can summarizes what has happened recently in the MOOC stream, making progress comprehensible to participants who have not been following all of the details. If they are kept up to date, a project’s landing page and Roadmap also serve as a sort of “wrapper”, telling people what resources they can expect to find in the class and how they can participate and contribute. Rationale: The wrapper must check the public summaries of the #GROOC #edX class from time to time to make sure that they accurately represent the facts on the ground. Resolution: According to the theory proposed by Yochai Benkler, for free/open “commons-based” projects to work, it is vital to have both: The ability to contribute small pieces; Something that stitches those pieces together @coases-penguin. The wrapper helps perform this integrative stitching function, which is often much more challenging than the job of breaking things down into pieces or just doing one of the small pieces. Rif: "The peeragogy Handbook"

Title: Untitled

Assignment 2.1 ☉ Learning City Point "Identify a Learning Challenge" Status: Done ✔ Suggested Due Date: 2/23/2016 Title: ♫ Peeragogical approch to music Education ♫ Context: Schools of Music, Conservatories, Public and private area. Problem: Often, piano students are frustrated by difficult of learning music. They play their music over and over, hoping that they will eventually get it right. Then, when they continue to have difficulty, they give up, believing that they are simply not talented. While talent is certainly an important aspect of success at the piano, in many cases such talent to emerge it needs to be tickled in different pedagogical approaches and methods for each of us. The following research is my contribution in order to Design and Development - Peeragogical Educational Technology- applied on musical studies. Why it is so challenging and why it is important: The people are free-range learners. Formal learning takes place in classrooms; informal learning happens everywhere. A workscape is a learning ecology. As the environment of learning, a workscape includes the workplace. In fact, a workscape has no boundaries. No two workscapes are alike. Your workscape may include a dedicated area at school or, thanks to new technologies hypothetically everywhere. My workscape and class project for example It will be design in a public park by reinventing the space itself. Developing this "Urban learning Point" concept it will increase our common city's values and and learning opportunities. The challenge is to create and protect this open environment. In an ideal Workscape, piano students can easily find training "locally or on-line", information and exercise they need, learning is fluid. “Tell me and I forget, teach me and I may remember, involve me and I learn.” ― Benjamin Franklin What’s Next: References & links: - Main Italian Open Project - peeragogy.org

Title: Untitled

Assignment 1.1 ☉ Learning City Point Ed Tech Then and Now: Status: In progress ✔ Suggested Due Date: Find an example of current (or recent) educational technology and try it out yourself: Now, think back to a technology which made an impression on you in your own learning experience (earlier technology): ................... Analyze the two technologies according to the following instructions. For the deliverable: For both the current and the earlier technology, give a quick description of each technology for those who might not be familiar with it and ideally link to information about it. Who was the intended primary audience and what does the user do when s/he uses the technology? Then answer the following questions:&nbsp; What do you think are some of the author’s goals regarding the technology? Does the technology direct the learner toward a specific goal or is it more open-ended? How and what might the learner learn from interacting with the technology? How specifically does it seek to engage the learner? How does it seek to motivate the learner? Based on your experience, did the technology meet its goals? Why or why not? Did it have other potentially unintentional effects (either positive or negative)? Choose one aspect of the experience that is common to both technologies. For instance, maybe both technologies (old and new) ask learners to complete practice problems. Or, maybe both have a user interface that allows the learner so see his or her progress. Next, compare the two experiences; tell us about differences and similarities. Were there other differences and similarities (not necessarily about a common experience) that you found to be especially striking? Tell us more. Overall, did you find one technology that was especially thought-provoking? Let us know your thinking.&nbsp; “Tell me and I forget, teach me and I may remember, involve me and I learn.” ― Benjamin Franklin What’s Next: References & links: - Main Italian Open Project ⇄ peeragogy.org

Title: Untitled

Assignment 2.2 ☉ Project pitch "WorST Intervention ever" Status: In progress Suggested Due Date: Now that you have your learning challenge, it is time to start brainstorming. Yes, of course you will think about the best way to respond to your learning challenge, but now it's time to approach it from a different angle. Right now, we want you to think about the worst intervention ever for your learning challenge .&nbsp; Here are just a few of the questions you may want to consider :&nbsp; How can you make things as difficult as possible for your learners?&nbsp;How can you design an intervention that will make it hard or undesirable for them to learn? How can you make the worst assessment possible? How can you make it hard for teachers or students to understand their progress? Do not just put up barriers; instead try to be counterproductive.&nbsp; Be creative! There is a method to our madness and we will tell you about it. However, first we want you to try this fun thought exercise.&nbsp; For the deliverable : Explain how this terrible intervention addresses your learning challenge. Why is it the worst intervention ever?&nbsp; Please include a picture or any other visual material if relevant. This will help your classmates understand why your intervention is the worst fit for your learning challenge.&nbsp;

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/assigment/compiti6-1
Title: Untitled

Assignment 6.1 ☉ Project pitch "Questions for Research" Status: Done ✔ Co-edit by Fabrizio Terzi & Federico Monaco Note: If you want your work to be considered for the live event, the deadline is earlier, as you will want to submit your final project by 3/27/16, 5:00 PM UTC. Researching an educational intervention is not always a priority depending on the type of project, but it serves a variety of important purposes. One is to learn about how new types of technology can improve learning and engagement, thereby advancing the educational technology field. But even if that’s not your goal, research on learning outcomes or best practices in implementation can encourage people to choose your product and help them use it more effectively . Were there learning gains over time in content knowledge or skills? Students identified laboratory classes, or practicals, as the main place where skills and knowledge were developed. This suggests that learning with new digital tools should focus on enhancing and potentially increasing the practical components of subjects. But practical classes are under threat. Student time in costly laboratory classes is being cut along with budgets to train properly laboratory tutors. While lectures are relatively cheap to deliver, musical students are saying they have a narrow focus on content knowledge and practice techniques. Students are uniquely placed to comment on the learning outcomes of formal & informal learning. They have experienced the curriculum and instruments. And as efforts to reform and provide this technology, students’ perception of their learning gains can greatly inform this. Conservatories of Music help students learn. But students can help music educators learn too. What types of projects did the technology enable students to complete? The Gate" or "Learning City point" project intend to act as Public local and online open space to contributions from scholars and citizen belonging systems thinking. The setting of the space in the park, is intended to be explicitly inter-trans-disciplinary, and expression of a "mesh" vision and attentive in identify and describe the processes of co-generation and recursion in community of practice . In addition, those who are doing their project goals, the public space is designed as a meeting and streaming performance dedicated to musical studies, with a special focus on theoretical frameworks, models, and field research on the specific areas of Education. How did teachers feel about incorporating the technology into their curriculum? Schooling still operates in the 19th century. We need to revolutionize everything about schooling. Technologically, much of what needs to change is less front-end than the back-end systems. From taking attendance to tracking free and reduced-price lunch to data analytics around special education, it is all pretty primitive. We also must make our systems of delivering education more openly available so that innovation can occur. In other words, we need more open-source intellectual property so that worldwide we improve schooling faster and more efficiently. In general, technology enhances student outcomes by forcing us to make our processes more explicit. So much of what we do is intuitive — we get into habits based on what has worked in the past, and those habits aren't always the best way to do things going forward. The more we try to automate what we do, the more we have to take all of those habits and assumptions and spell them out to the point that a computer can make sense of them. Yes, we get the benefit of having technology do things that would otherwise have to be done manually, and we get analytics to help us make better decisions, but we also get a clearer view of ourselves. Technology forces us to be brutally honest with ourselves about what we do, how we spend our time and resources, and what outcomes we achieve. It makes it hard to hide behind assumptions. We're currently getting technology to work for us in this way on a number of fronts. We're redesigning the way we record live piano and other digital instruments, grades, attendance, and classroom management. We're professional development, and performance management data into systems that can merge that information with our scholar outcomes. We're just finishing up a project that takes information about buildings, sections, staff, co-located schools and a ton of other constraints and gives principals suggestions on how to most efficiently schedule classes and maximize student opportunities for extracurricular classes. We are particularly excited about a newly developed system that augments educators’ observations with inferences from machine learning. To our knowledge, this is rarely if ever done in brick-and-mortar schools, particularly at the pre-k to 12 level. The system uses state-of-the-art modeling procedures to create interactive data visualizations that go far beyond dashboards. Dashboards aggregate data. Our system distills data into actionable insights. Read on Google Doc

Title: Untitled

Project blog: "Peer to Peer feedback" 17 Feb 2016 ☉ @Bonnie Taylor (isdiva) Learning by sharing: Thank you for inviting feedback on your project. Here are my responses to the feedback prompts: Does the participant clearly state the problem? I infer from your statement of the problem that you see the challenge as being this: piano students become discouraged from continuing to devote time to develop expertise in the skill of piano playing. You mention learning music” but it seems to me you are specifically referring to learning to perform music, which is a slightly different idea. On the other hand, later in your description to refer to the need to cultivate talent (skill?) in other ways besides what is already done, using a different pedagogical approach/method. That is a different problem, though. The first seems to be presented as a motivation problem (for the student), and the other problem seems to be insufficient teaching technique (for the teacher, whether that teacher is an expert or a near-peer). I am not clear on which problem you are really intending to address. Does the participant describe the setting and/or who the learners are? The context of learning to perform music can be gained from the description, although it might have been helpful to have more description of the types of learners who are expected to receive the most assistance from what you are planning to do. Will “all piano students” equally benefit from your proposal, or would some types of students (younger, older, more novice, economically disadvantaged, and so on) be more likely to benefit? How thoughtfully does the participant explain why this area is challenging? This part is not clear to me. Why is it challenging, for example, to motivate students to keep practicing even when they become discouraged and do not feel they have the talent to continue? Or why is it challenging for teachers to recognize that talent can be encouraged in different ways? In either case, the solution you describe (which may be premature, and probably does not belong in this section) does not appear to be directly connected to the challenges you present. Perhaps consider including an example of a person who struggled with the problem you present, describing some of the barriers or obstacles they faced. Has the participant backed up their assertion with experiences, observations, etc.? It would be helpful to see a bit more informal description of your research instead of a hyperlink to an open source document. Another suggestion is to guide your reader to the part of the document that is most relevant to your presentation. If it is really just the whole document, a summary of what the document says would suffice. What other insights, if any, can you provide that would help your classmate refine or develop their focus? Perhaps back away a bit from jumping to the solution of redesigning a workspace at this point of your idea development process. Consider adding some information that would acknowledge why the problem has not already been addressed in the past (it is expensive, time-consuming, labor-intensive, and so on). These might form the motivation for your audience to consider how your eventual proposal is a good option for the future. Phase-1 Read "Il Portale" A New Urban Concept. 2/3 Feb 2016 ☉ Learning City Point Abstract: « ...Ci sono cose per cui vale la pena impegnarsi, tutti quanti, grandi e piccoli. Una di queste cose è la propria città, amandola e inventandola ogni giorno. La città siamo noi, i nostri desideri e la nostra visione del futuro. Tecnologia, natura, accoglienza, sapere, sostenibilità, turismo e tradizione. In una parola: personalità e a Bergamo di certo non mancano ». La finalità del progetto "Il Portale" o "Learning City Point" è di re-immaginare lo spazio pubblico cittadino e offrire un punto d'accesso e condivisione d' informazioni on-line e accesso alla rete per i tutti i cittadini, studiosi e volontari. Il completamento dell'opera nel parco e la sua gestione come "Learning point" è destinato ad essere esplicitamente di carattere inter-trans-disciplinare e culturale, espressione di una visione della città condivisa e attenta a identificare e descrivere i processi di co-generazione. L'intento è quello di fornire uno spazio di condivisione,un punto di riferimento cittadino, per ricercatori e chiunque sia attivo alla vita cittadina. Inviteremo diversi partecipanti provenienti da diversi paesi, con particolare attenzione nel dare voce a coloro che indagano i settori di ricerca applicata e sperimentazione in ambienti "Open Education". Fase-1 Read The role of Wrapper in this project. 16 Jen 2016 ☉ Engaging The wrapper helps perform this integrative stitching function, which is often much more challenging than the job of breaking things down into pieces or just doing one of the small pieces.... Fase-2 Read #MIT Coursewere 29 Gen 2016 ☉ Co-Creating This project-based course explores educational technologies and the theories underlying their development through interviews with experts in the field. week-1 Join Most influential theories of learning 04 Feb 2016 ☉ Peer-Learning Learning is defined as a process that brings together personal and environmental experiences and influences for acquiring, enriching or modifying one’s knowledge, skills, values, attitudes, behaviour and world views. Learning theories develop hypotheses that describe how this process takes place. The scientific study of learning started in earnest at the dawn of the 20th century. The major concepts and theories of learning include behaviourist theories, cognitive psychology, constructivism, social constructivism, experiential learning, multiple intelligence, and situated learning theory and community of practice. week-1 UNESCO

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/blog/1
Title: Untitled

Wrapper role Definition: Wrapper Problem: In a very active course, it can be effectively impossible to stay up to date with all of the details. Not everyone will be able to attend every meeting, follow forum discussion, and project participants can easily get lost and drift away. The experience can be even worse for newcomers. Joining a course already going can feel like trying to get aboard a rapidly moving vehicle. If you’ve taken time off, you may feel like things have moved on so far that they cannot catch up. Solution: A project contributor can summarizes what has happened recently in the GROOC stream, making progress comprehensible to participants who have not been following all of the details. If they are kept up to date, a project’s landing page and Roadmap also serve as a sort of “wrapper”, telling people what resources they can expect to find in the class and how they can participate and contribute. Rationale: The wrapper must check the public summaries of the #GROOC #edX class from time to time to make sure that they accurately represent the facts on the ground. Resolution: According to the theory proposed by Yochai Benkler, for free/open “commons-based” projects to work, it is vital to have both: The ability to contribute small pieces; Something that stitches those pieces together @coases-penguin. The wrapper helps perform this integrative stitching function, which is often much more challenging than the job of breaking things down into pieces or just doing one of the small pieces. Rif: "The peeragogy Handbook"

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/groups/1
Title: Untitled

Peeragogy Community Unpeeragogical Facilitator: Fabrizio Terzi Actual members engagement Peeragogy is a flexible framework of techniques for peer learning and peer knowledge production. Where as pedagogy deals with the transmission of knowledge from teachers to students, peeragogy is what people use to produce and apply knowledge together. The strength of peeragogy is its flexibility and scalability. The learning mind-set and strategies that we are uncovering in the Peeragogy project can be applied in classrooms, hackerspaces, organizations, wikis, and interconnected collaborations across an entire society. Resources: UnPeeragogy Notebook. Rif: edX-week2

============================================================

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/groups/2
Title: Untitled

The Thrive|ryders (OET) Open Educational Training for Social Impact @ BergamoHub Fabrizio Terzi Dessi Luciano Actual members engagement Local community engagement Participation has become critical in sustaining online Communities of Practice (COPs). Evidence from other fields shows that facilitators can help communities to thrive. Through effective facilitation, members can become active participants in their communities. We argue that members' social identity is a key for members to become more attached and more active. Further, as members are involved in communication and information exchanges, technology becomes an important aspect of COPs. Therefore, perceived ease of use of communication as well as information functionality become important drivers for participation. Resources: BergamoHub. Rif: edX-week2

My Course Project Group: Team members: Fabrizio Terzi Bonnie Taylor Actual members engagement ᴥ Co-Creating: ☀ Engaging: ₪ Designing: ↝ Scaling: ✿ Resourcing: Assesing: Participation has become critical in sustaining online Communities of Practice (COPs). Evidence from other fields shows that facilitators can help communities to thrive. Through effective facilitation, members can become active participants in their communities. We argue that members' social identity is a key for members to become more attached and more active. Further, as members are involved in communication and information exchanges, technology becomes an important aspect of COPs. URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/groups/4
Title: Untitled

Peeragogy Community Unpeeragogical Facilitator: Fabrizio Terzi Actual members engagement Peeragogy is a flexible framework of techniques for peer learning and peer knowledge production. Where as pedagogy deals with the transmission of knowledge from teachers to students, peeragogy is what people use to produce and apply knowledge together. The strength of peeragogy is its flexibility and scalability. The learning mind-set and strategies that we are uncovering in the Peeragogy project can be applied in classrooms, hackerspaces, organizations, wikis, and interconnected collaborations across an entire society. Resources: UnPeeragogy Notebook. Rif: edX-week2

Unit ⚶u1.v1.s1 Welcome to Unit 1! In this unit, we will consider the history of educational technology, introduce the theory of constructionism, and look at two projects inspired by it.&nbsp; Our first live event, a Reddit " Ask Me Anything" with Professor Klopfer, will take place on Thursday, February 4, 2016 at 3 PM UTC. You will receive access information prior to the event.&nbsp; History of Educational Technology &nbsp;- We will explore how technologies used in education have (or have not) changed the content and procedure of learning and teaching. Constructionism & Related&nbsp;Educational Theories: Professor&nbsp;Susan Yoon discusses&nbsp;where the theory of constructionism came from and how it relates to the design of current educational technology.&nbsp; Logo: Professor&nbsp;Hal Abelson presents a&nbsp;case study of an early programming language that enabled students to work with computers in a different way. Scratch Programming: Professor&nbsp;Mitch Resnick and Ricarose Roque&nbsp;tell us about a modern-day descendant of Logo and give examples of how it is used.&nbsp; We will be reading "Most Influential Theories of Learning" (a brief overview put together by UNESCO) and a section of the U.S. Department of Education Ed Tech Developer's Guide: A Primer for Software Developers, Startups, and Entrepreneurs.Participants who wish to dive deeper may read Edith Ackermann's paper ""Piaget’s Constructivism, Papert’s Constructionism: What’s the difference?." Constructionism Theory In this unit, we will consider the history of educational technology, introduce the theory of constructionism, and look at two projects inspired by i Dr. Hal Abelson, Class of 1922 Professor of Computer Science and Engineering at MIT, tells the story of how the programming language Logo came to be. He sets the stage for why children making things with computers was such a novel idea at the time and explains the Logo philosophy.Hal mentions Seymour Papert's paper "Teaching Children Thinking1 Scratch Appearances by: : Susan Yoon, Hal Abelson, Mitch Resnick, and Ricarose Roque.

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/unita/u2
Title: 

Unit ⚶u2.v1.s1 Welcome to Unit 2! Professor Klopfer introduces the question of what learning looks like and the idea of moving from novice to expert status. The role of a teacher or educator is to scaffold that process of deep learning to bring learners to a state of mastery, and technology is one tool that can help do that. Overview & What is Learning?: Professor Klopfer explores&nbsp;what learning looks like and what it means to become an expert. Teaching for Understanding:&nbsp; Judy Perry, who you met in Unit 1, talks with Professor David Perkins about the Teaching for Understanding approach,&nbsp;a framework for planning activities that will encourage deep learning. SimCalc: Dr. Jeremy Roschelle tells us about SimCalc,&nbsp;a software tool for math learning, and how it was scaled up. Cognitive Tutors:&nbsp; Professor Kurt VanLehn introduces intelligent tutoring systems, explaining how they work and&nbsp;how they can help guide students welcome to week two David Perkins, Carl H. Pforzheimer, Jr. Research Professor of Teaching and Learning at Harvard Graduate School of Education, explains why all educators want to teach for understanding and how this is different from routine learning. The challenge is designing lessons that get students to "think with what they know." He presents his framework created to help teachers support this deep learning process. Dr. Jeremy Roschelle, co-director of the Center for Technology in Learning at SRI International, tells the story of SimCalc . By starting with graphs instead of equations, SimCalc draws people in using the learning theory of multiple representations. Jeremy describes how the design of SimCalc changed as his team understood more about how people learn math. Professor Kurt VanLehn, the Diane and Gary Tooker Chair for Effective Education in Science, Technology, Engineering and Math at Arizona State University, explains what an intelligent tutoring system is and describes the varying levels of sophistication and interaction that exist in these systems. He talks about what it takes to create an intelligent tutoring system and how it can help students learn by providing useful feedback. Appearances by: : Susan Yoon, Hal Abelson, Mitch Resnick, and Ricarose Roque.

============================================================

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/unita/u3
Title: 

Unit ⚶u3.v1.s1 Welcome to Unit 3! We explore the idea of active learning. This concept includes students' freedom to make decisions about how they explore a topic, and their reflections on those learning experiences. Overivew & Active Learning - Prof. Klopfer gets us started by defining active learning and explains why it can help students gain better understanding. Next, we will take&nbsp;a look at some technologies that can enable active learning Geniverse: Dr. Paul Horwitz introduces us to Geniverse, an online environment for learning genetics for high school biology. This first case study shows how simulations can be a tool to stimulate active learning. StarLogo Nova: Daniel Wendel presents StarLogo Nova, a tool that allows students to do simulated experiments. Wendy Huang tells us how StarLogo Nova is implemented in real classrooms.&nbsp; The Lifelong Kindergarten:&nbsp; Professor Mitchel Resnick, who we met earlier in the course, reflects on the evolution of constructionism and discusses a few projects from his lab.&nbsp; Constructionist Technologies: Professor Matthew Berland talks about projects he has worked on that are inspired by constructionism. Non-cognitive Skills: This unit includes a TED Talk by Professor Angela Duckworth. She reveals why&nbsp;grit and persistence are as important as content knowledge and skill building. Scot Osterweil describes his work on The Logical Journey of the Zoombinis and the process of designing activities to help students persist in the face of challenges.&nbsp; Overview and Active Learning Prof. Klopfer defines "simulation" and provides examples. Dr. Paul Horwitz, Senior Scientist at the Concord Consortium, introduces the Concord Consortium (its work and its philosophy) and details his own journey from being a physicist to creating educational technologies. He talks about how science is a "game" but isn't taught that way, and how this understanding has influenced his work. Get an introduction to Geniverse by watching the video. . Paul describes the GenScope project and its affect on kids' motivation as well as their test scores. Professional development and a flexible curriculum were found to be essential as the project morphed into Biologica, and later Geniverse. In all iterations, implementation strategies were key areas to focus on. Paul talks more generally about why educational technology and simulations are important for science learning, in terms of both content and practices. He also discusses strategies for facilitating group reflection and making connections to the real world. This segment is a bonus. Daniel Wendel, a project manager/software developer in Eric's lab, talks about the affordances of StarLogo software and the wide variety of agent-based systems that can be built with it. He describes the software design, curriculum designs, and moments of learning that students have had while working with it. Wendy Huang, a curriculum developer and program manager at Eric's lab, talks about the many ways in which teachers and students are utilizing StarLogo Nova, from presenting simulations, to modifying them, to creating them. She describes some of the most effective teacher training methods and implementation approaches that enable use of the StarLogo technology into classrooms. sWendy Huang, a curriculum developer and program manager at Eric's lab, talks about the many ways in which teachers and students are utilizing StarLogo Nova, from presenting simulations, to modifying them, to creating them. She describes some of the most effective teacher training methods and implementation approaches that enable use of the StarLogo technology into classrooms. Angela Lee Duckworth, now a professor at the University of Pennsylvania, shares her experience teaching math to seventh graders in a New York public school. She quickly realized that IQ wasn’t the only thing separating the successful students from those who struggled. Here, she explains her theory of “grit” as a predictor of success. Judy Perry talks with Scot Osterweil about how non-cognitive skills can be learned through play given the right factors. He connects active learning and the acquisition of skills to the overall experience of games. Thank you #edX #MITx

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/unita/u4
Title: 

Unit ⚶u4.v1.s1 Welcome to Unit 4! We consider the idea of social, or collaborative, learning. Note: This unit is two weeks long. On Monday, March 14, 2016 at 4:00 PM UTC, our Community TAs will host a live event where participants will have the opportunity to receive feedback on their pitches. You can find out more in the Unit 4 forum area. Access information will be provided closer to the date. Overview & Collaborative Learning:&nbsp; Professor Klopfer introduces the concept of communities of practice, meaning groups of people with a common interest who want to learn about a certain topic or skill by working together. This kind of group can&nbsp;provide many benefits to learning and teaching. Samba Schools : Professor Mitchel Resnick, Dr. Cynthia Solomon, and Professor Yasmin Kafai take a closer&nbsp;look at samba schools as a great example of a community of practice. Experts on Collaborative Learning :&nbsp; Scot Osterweil, Professor Yasmin Kafai, Professor&nbsp; Kurt Squire , Professor&nbsp; Barry Fishman , Dr. Jeremy Roschelle, and Professor&nbsp; Sasha Barab &nbsp; share their thoughts about collaborative learning (also known as group or social learning).&nbsp; Vanished: Caitlin Feeley and Scot Osterweil discuss&nbsp;an alternate reality game, Vanished , that encouraged players to solve problems together online. Online Learning: Dr. Justin Reich and Dr. J. Philipp Schmidt provide&nbsp;illustrative examples of how people are taking advantage of the Internet to learn together.&nbsp; Overview of collaborative learning Seymour Papert was intrigued and fascinated by Samba schools; Professor Mitchel Resnick (LEGO Papert Professor of Learning Research at MIT), Dr. Cynthia Solomon (associated with MIT), Professor Yasmin Kafai (University of Pennsylvania) help us understand why. These learning communities bring together people of mixed ages and skill levels to support all learners, resulting in amazing dance performances. It is an interesting model of social learning that is very different from contemporary schools. We present this case study here to inspire you to think differently about collaborative and social learning; it is not just students working in small groups in a classroom. A variety of education researchers talk about what they see as the benefits of collaborative learning. They point out a number of tools and learning environments that support and embody collaborative learning, as well as discussing their own related work. Scot explains that he does not think of collaborative and individual learning as completely separate (1:24 in the video). Caitlin Feeley, a project manager at Professor Klopfer's lab (Scheller Teacher Education Program/The Education Arcade) and Scot Osterweil talk about Vanished, an alternate reality game in which middle school students all over the world worked together to solve a fictional scientific mystery. They utilized online forums to crack codes, work with scientists, and complete a variety of authentic science-based puzzles, all in service of changing students' attitudes and interest in science. Dr. Justin Reich, now Executive Director of the Teaching Systems Lab at MIT, gives a brief history of online learning experiences and MOOCs, then talks about self-pacing, community building, and other factors that are important in MOOC design. While certain things about online courses are innovative, just being online does not inherently change the way courses are taught. However, there is potential to make learning accessible to a wider variety of students. Dr. Justin Reich, now Executive Director of the Teaching Systems Lab at MIT, gives a brief history of online learning experiences and MOOCs, then talks about self-pacing, community building, and other factors that are important in MOOC design. While certain things about online courses are innovative, just being online does not inherently change the way courses are taught. However, there is potential to make learning accessible to a wider variety of students. Thank you #edX #MITx

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/unita/u5
Title: 

Unit ⚶u1.v1.s1 Welcome to Unit 5! How do we understand what learners are understanding? We use assessment. This unit will help you discover more about the purpose of assessment, as well as methods.&nbsp; Overview & Defining Assessment: What do students think about assessment?&nbsp;In this section, students talk about what they think assessments are, what they look like, and what they can measure. Next, Professor Jody Clarke-Midura explains the differences between formative, summative, and performance assessments Perspectives on Assessment: Professor Jim Gee, Dr. Malcolm Bauer, Dr. Edys Quellmalz, Dr. Bob Mislevy, and Dr. Kristen DiCerbo present their views on assessment and explore how technology is changing the field of educational assessment and how it may lead to improvements. Learning by Inquiry Inq-ITS, a virtual assessment environment centered around inquiry-based science activities. Choice-based Assessments:&nbsp; Professor Dan Schwartz discusses his work regarding assessing students' ability to make good choices Future of Assessment:&nbsp; Professor Jim Gee, Dr. Malcolm Bauer, Professor Ryan Baker, Dr. Bob Mislevy and Dr. Kristen DiCerbothink about how assessing content and skills will change as new standards and frameworks evolve We will be reading "Every Teacher's Guide to Assessment" ( an Edudemic article by Amanda Ronan). Those who wish to dive deeper may read an excerpt from Beyond Basic Skills: The Role of Performance Assessment in Achieving 21st Century Standards of Learning .&nbsp; Appearances by : Pembroke High School students, Oren Klopfer, Maya Klopfer, Jody Clarke-Midura, Jim Gee, Malcolm Bauer, Edys Quellmalz, Bob Mislevy, Kristen DiCerbo, Janice Gobert, Dan Schwartz, Ryan Baker Professor James Paul Gee (Jim), Regents' Professor and Fulton Presidential Chair of Literature Studies at Arizona State University, sees assessment as a natural part of learning if you view learning as progress through time. Given the ability of technology to collect large amounts of data, he talks about the importance of assessing learners on multiple variables and providing actionable feedback. He also touches on how video games successfully incorporate this type of assessment. Dr. Malcolm Bauer, Managing Senior Research Scientist at ETS (Educational Testing Service), sees assessment as the collection of data and observations, and the making of inferences about what people think and can do. He talks about what current assessments are good at measuring, what their limitations are, and what changes technology can bring about. Dr. Edys Quellmalz (Director of Technology Enhanced Assessments and Learning Systems in the Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics program at WestEd) discusses how technology has enabled students to present and express their understandings in a variety of ways. Dr. Kristen DiCerbo, Principal Research Scientist at Pearson, sees assessments as a way of gathering evidence about what students know and can do. She talks about the many different purposes for assessments, and explains how we are currently on the shore of the "digital ocean" when it comes to collecting educational data. Appearances by: : Susan Yoon, Hal Abelson, Mitch Resnick, and Ricarose Roque.

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/video/a
Title: Untitled

Muhammad Yunus: In 2006, Muhammad Yunus, an economist from Bangladesh, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of his efforts to combat global poverty and empower millions through a social innovation now known as micro-finance. In this GROOC interview, he shares his experience with scaling the Grameen Bank and measuring its social impact, as well as his thoughts about leadership, social imagination and human connection. Muhammad Yunus is the Grameen founder. He was born on 28th June, 1940 in the village of Bathua, Chittagong, the business centre of what was then Eastern Bengal. He was the 3rd of 14 children of whom five died in infancy. His father was a successful goldsmith. He always encouraged his sons to seek higher education. But his biggest influence was Sufia Khatun – his mother, who always helped the poor people that knocked on their door. This inspired him to commit himself to eradication of poverty. His early childhood years were spent in the village. His family moved to the city of Chittagong, where his father had the jewelery business in 1947. Rif: edCX

Gabe Mott: Gabe Mott is Chief Operating Officer for Aspire , a social enterprise whose mission is to provide economically challenged, malnourished populations with high protein and micronutrient-rich food solutions derived from the supply and development of insects and insect-based products. In this GROOC interview, he describes his team’s winning journey competing in the Hult Prize competition and everything they have learned since being awarded $1 million in seed funding. Mary Gordon: Mary Gordon, is a Canadian educator, author, child advocate, parenting expert and award-winning social entrepreneur, who believes in the power of empathy. URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/video/d
Title: Untitled

Eric Klopfer Klopfer’s research focuses on the development and use of computer games and simulations for building understanding of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. The games that he works on are designed to build understanding of scientific practices and concepts as well as critical knowledge, using both mobile and web-delivered game platforms. In the realm of simulations, Klopfer’s work focuses on students understanding complex systems through, and connecting computer programming with, scientific practice, critical thinking, and real-world issues. He is the co-author of the books, Adventures in Modeling and The More We Know, as well as the author of Augmented Learning. Klopfer is also the co-founder and past president of the non-profit Learning Games Network. Rif: edX-week1

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/video/e
Title: Untitled

Scot Osterweil Scot Osterweil is the Creative Director of the Education Arcade and a research director in the MIT Comparative Media Studies/Writing Program. He is a designer of award-winning educational games, working in both academic and commercial environments, and his work has focused on what is authentically playful in challenging academic subjects. He has designed games for computers, handheld devices, and multi-player on-line environments. He is the creator of the acclaimed Zoombinis series of math and logic games, and leads a number of projects in the Education Arcade, including the MIT/Smithsonian curated game, Vanished (environmental science), Labyrinth(math), Kids Survey Network (data and statistics), Caduceus (medical science), iCue (history and civics) and the Hewlett Foundation’s Open Language Learning Initiative (ESL). He is a founding member of the Learning Games Network (www.learninggamesnetwork.org). Rif: edX-week1

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/MITx/pages/video/f
Title: Untitled

Judy Perry Judy oversees design, development, and research for several projects involving games and simulations, and their integration into formal or informal learning settings. Her work includes overseeing the TaleBlazer software platform, a toolkit and support materials which enable users to make and play their own location-based, augmented reality (AR) games. Judy’s research interests include location-based games, ubiquitous “casual” games, mobile games, and more generally with digital-materials which foster engagement with STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics). Judy also leads professional development training workshops for educators who want to implement STEP Lab projects. She also enjoys collaborating with other institutions (including zoos, nature centers, libraries, science museums, living history museums, and K-12 classrooms) to develop experimental learning offerings. Prior to becoming a researcher at MIT, her work included television and web production, and content development for educational toys. She holds a B.A. in American Studies from Yale University, and an Ed.M. in Technology Innovation, and Education (T.I.E.) from the Harvard Graduate School of Education. Rif: edX-week2

Title: Untitled

Stanford OpenEdX "Changing the Global Course of Learning" Open source, open science, open data, open access, open education, open learning -- this course provides an introduction to the important concept of openness from a variety of perspectives, including education, publishing, librarianship, economics, politics, and more, and asks you to discover what it means to you. Open Knowledge is international and multi-institutional, bringing together instructors and students from Canada, Ghana, Mexico, the United States, and the rest of the world. It will challenge you take control of your own education, to determine your own personal learning objectives, to contribute to the development of the curriculum, to reflect on your progress, to learn new digital skills, and to take a leadership role in the virtual classroom. It will also provide you with the opportunity to connect with colleagues from different countries and professions, and to better understand areas where your interests overlap and where unexpected distincts exist. We hope you’ll consider taking this journey with us. Rif: edX-week2

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/projects/fabrizio-project-2
Title: Untitled

S.I.A.R Sensory Immertion Augmented Reality Abstract: The research model presented here derives from the development of a magnetic gyroscopic electro-mechanical apparatus in the environment of an Open Innovation Research Technology Project (S.I.A.R.) . I am convinced that this model can be improved through the mindful sharing of knowledge and experience among researchers. The Human Computer Interaction (HCI) applied in engineering computer science research has permitted us to develop and discover new technology and refine our technological approach on an almost daily basis. The findings presented here, build upon the concept of the cardanic gyroscopic suspension "Gimpal" mechanism described it in detail by the Italian Renaissance mathematician Girolamo Cardano (1501-1576), who was in turn informed by the Greek inventor Philo Byzantium(280-220) and Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519). Research Paradigm: Our senses determinate everything that exists in our world but that doesn’t necessarily mean that’s the end of our world. We have to embrace knowledge that’s unconventional that’s in the unseen. And if we can wire it in our brain first, than what has always existed will now be seen by us. The Why: My greatest desire is to establish an NGO. that would allow the poorest children to imagine and build a new future. For this reason S.I.A.R. become my financial leverage for the foundations of an Open Innovation Technology Academy Institute where children, can grow and imagine a different future through the creation of new technology and Paragogy (peer tutoring and learning.) Only for members

URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/projects/fabrizio-project-4
Title: Untitled

Bergamo Hub ☼Seed Project☼ Learning City Center Lab Abstract: We believe that there is no shortage of good ideas for solving the problems of our time, but there is a need to introduce new socio-economic and education, in public spaces dedicated to their development and sustainability planning. Bergamo HUB will be designed and engineered to meet this requirement. we decided to propose to the destination city of the former Central thermoelectric via Deste Spalenga Bergamo ITALY spaces equipped with all the tools necessary support meeting social, cultural, creative and technology to the city. I want to allow the talent and creativity of the citizens of Bergamo to find the best conditions in order to realize their ideas, project proposals and aspirations. But above all, spaces for meaningful encounters, exchange and inspiration, full of different people will do amazing things together. Bergamo HUB will be part of an international network of beautiful physical spaces where entrepreneurs, and creative professionals will have access to all the resources, let inspired by the work of others, have innovative ideas, develop useful relationships and individual tify new market opportunities and development. It will be a space dedicated citizen innovation and social entrepreneurship and the people who promote. here you can meet people very different, contractors and operators non-profit organizations, professionals, young people, students, educators, designers and experts in different sectors, all united by the desire to improve and enhance the lives of community sharing ideas and challenges of the future. Title: Untitled

Digital Gallery 3D Digital Art Being able to express ideas and feelings playing with colours and forms is what inspires and motivates me take digital brushes to give free rein to the imagination. I am inspired by the everyday, by small moments and big ideas. I love working in the digital medium because it lets me take these ideas and present them to you the same way I see them in my head—as places you could walk into and explore. I believe the digital creations is finding its place in the art world, and that artists should use, value and enjoy all available means of creative expression. I hope that artists and art lovers everywhere continue to push the boundaries of what constitutes a fine art. FineArt America

Title: Untitled

Bergamo Hub ☼Seed Project☼ Learning City Center Lab Abstract: We believe that there is no shortage of good ideas for solving the problems of our time, but there is a need to introduce new socio-economic and education, in public spaces dedicated to their development and sustainability planning. Bergamo HUB will be designed and engineered to meet this requirement. we decided to propose to the destination city of the former Central thermoelectric via Deste Spalenga Bergamo ITALY spaces equipped with all the tools necessary support meeting social, cultural, creative and technology to the city. I want to allow the talent and creativity of the citizens of Bergamo to find the best conditions in order to realize their ideas, project proposals and aspirations. But above all, spaces for meaningful encounters, exchange and inspiration, full of different people will do amazing things together. Bergamo HUB will be part of an international network of beautiful physical spaces where entrepreneurs, and creative professionals will have access to all the resources, let inspired by the work of others, have innovative ideas, develop useful relationships and individual tify new market opportunities and development. When the community finds it has a complex problem and is struggling with possible solutions and there is a diverse group of people that can be brought together to help work on it then Open Space Technology (OST) is a great option to try. URL: https://fabrizio.pyragogy.org/projects/fabrizio-project-9
Title: Untitled

Bergamo Hub ☼Seed Project☼ Learning City Center Lab Vision: Catalyze the evolution of individuals and organizations making a profoundly positive impact on people and in Bergamo. Mission: Put into action the best ideas, systems and technology that creates a more just and sustainable city. Deliver unique impact by providing a physical home that integrates local communities in social innovation. Pollinate the top ideas, lessons and opportunities among the sub-groups of experts in Bergamo, creating new companies and jobs, while firmly connecting our city with the global networks of change-makers. Values: Action: Beyond simply appreciating new ideas, and models pioneered elsewhere, we focus on implementation and measurable outcomes. Service: We focus on supporting people and organizations making positive change in the world, honoring concepts of reciprocity, and contributing to activities that strengthen our community. Entrepreneurial Spirit: Foster the creativity, innovation, drive, determination and (multiple forms of) capital necessary to make new ideas come to fruition. Community: Provide a container and programming to integrate the diverse collection of people and organizations who share a common interest in collective impact on society and the environment. Actively promote and catalyze learning, sharing, new connections, and cross-disciplinary dialog, leading to collaboration. Launch Italian Project

Title: Attestazione di frequenza

Attestazione di frequenza Certificato di validazione professionale Congratulationi, Fabrizio Terzi! Hai lavorato duramente per ottenere il tuo certificato da Fondazione Et-Labora: condividilo con colleghi, amici e familiari per far conoscere ciò che hai imparato nella gestione Logistica e organizzazione di un magazzino. Certificato Verificato Supportato dalle seguenti organizzazioni Certifichiamo che Fabrizio Terzi Ha con successo ha completato il nostro corso di formazione professionale: MAGAZZINO E LOGISTICA 4.0: SOSTENIBILITA’ AMBIENTALE E SECURITY Un corso di studi di 150 ore offerto da regione Lombardia in collaborazione con Fondazione Et Labora Bergamo. Firmato da dott.ssa Bergamaschi Roberta Responsabile unità organizzativa Fondazione Et Labora (Bg) Certificazione rilasciata in Maggio 30, 2021 Valid Certificate ID 6a70cb00aaee4640bec8d02b6be4e363 Dote unica lavoro Regione Lombardia del 10/05/2021 - Codice identificativo: 29519772951977 Obbiettivi del corso Fornire ai partecipanti competenze progettuali, gestionali ed organizzative necessarie per intervenire in maniera coordinata sia sugli aspetti strutturali della logistica di magazzino sia sugli aspetti gestionali ed organizzativi, con lo scopo di aumentare l'efficienza e le prestazioni del magazzino, simulazioni di gestione d'impresa e di magazzino, business plan e documenti previsionali collegati. Il corso si rivolge a persone che operano nell’ area della logistica: direzione logistica, responsabili logistica, responsabili di magazzino, operatori ufficio magazzino, operatori di magazzino avanzati. Sede di Bergamo Via Andrea Moretti, 7/11 - Bergamo Tel: 035 225308 / 333 6349186 / 337 1292679 Email: bergamo@fondazioneetlabora.org Ringraziamenti personali Desidero ringraziare prima di tutto regione Lombardia per avermi concesso l'opportunità di frequentare un corso di riqualificazione professionale in cui ho potuto apprendere molto nel campo della logistica e incontrare persone davvero straordinarie. Un grazie speciale ai tutor "Giovanni Levi, Dario Roncelli, Lida Gherardi, Martello Maurizio, Emanuele Favarato ", alla loro professionalità e dedizione all'insegnamento. Hanno saputo egregiamente trasmetterci concetti, non sempre facili, e fornirci i migliori strumenti per essere nuovamente competitivi nella ricerca di una nuova occupazione. Grazie alla fondazione Et-Labora di Bergamo per aver progettato questo ottimo percorso formativo e a Linda Pesenti che con grande professionalità e gentilezza ci ha accompagnato durante tutto il percorso fornendoci un preziosissimo supporto. Fabrizio Terzi

Vedi credenziale Scuola Superiore Diploma di Perito Informatico 1994 - 2000 Istituto tecnico industriale "Pietro Paleocapa" 87/100 Certificato professionale in "Insegnamento online per educatori" British Columbia University: febbraio 2021 - agosto 2021 L'istruzione online è cresciuta e si è evoluta molto negli ultimi anni e la pandemia COVID-19 ha accelerato questo cambiamento. Navigare nell'ambiente online tuttavia può essere scoraggiante e difficile da gestire al meglio affrontando tutte le svariate esigenze degli studenti. Questo programma di certificazione professionale, è stato progettato per Educatori e amministratori di piattaforme educative al fine di rispondere a questi bisogni e a pianificare, sviluppare, implementare e fornire programmi online coinvolgenti e duraturi in modo efficace. Vedi credenziale Design Educational Technology MITx - Massachusetts Institute of Technology: gennaio 2016 - giugno 2016 Per essere efficaci, le tecnologie educative devono essere progettate sulla base di ciò che sappiamo su come le persone apprendono. Nelle sei unità di contenuto nell'arco di 24 settimane, ho potuto acquisire una comprensione sulle teorie e i modelli selezionati per l'apprendimento incorporati nella tecnologia educativa utilizzata oggi. Ho potuto lavorare al prototipo di un nuova tecnologia Educativa per l'apprendimento musicale basata sulla teoria "Peeragogica", ha cui diedi il nome; Il Portale Vedi credenziale Social Learning for Social Impact McGill University: aprile 2015 - luglio 2015 Il primo GROOCx organizzato online per l'apprendimento condiviso di gruppi di lavoro e ricerca. Il suo obbiettivo è stato principalmente ispirare la creazione di iniziative sociali capaci di generare un impatto a livello locale. È stato un bellissimo corso online aperto che ha coinvolto una rete mondiale di persone e gruppi che si preoccupano di creare un mondo migliore. Io sono Fabrizio e mi definisco un collaboratore non proprio convenzionale. Questo perchè oltre a dare sempre il meglio sul lavoro, ho la fortuna di poter amalgamare molte esperienze professionali estere e molta dedizione in tutto ciò che faccio. Amo la musica, blues e classica contemporanea sono senza dubbio i generi preferiti che prediligo suonare. Ho la passione per l'informatica e mi definiscono anche come "l'amico della porta accanto "smanettone" che chiami quando il Pc proprio non vuol saperne di funzionare". Studio per diletto l'apprendimento a distanza Peer to Peer e le tecnologie Open Source. Tra una pausa e l'altra mi piace vedere una partita di calcio con amici e fare quattro risate. Adoro viaggiare da solo e fotografare le meraviglie che incontro in ogni paese che visito e questo mi rende felice e carico quando rientro al lavoro. Al momento sono impegnato come volontario in progetti sociali ed educativi di ricerca che possano avere un impatto positivo per le generazioni future. -Learning on Open Educational Culture. Pianoforte e chitarra Bitcoin Photography Football Traveling Food & Beverage Testimonials Ho conosciuto Fabrizio in aula, come partecipante ad un corso di Logistica & Magazzino. Fin da subito si è rivelata una persona intelligente, perspicace, attenta e premurosa nei confronti dei propri compagni. I suoi apporti di idee e riflessioni, considerando anche la materia per lui "nuova", hanno dato un contributo realmente interessante; le sue domande, i suoi collegamenti, sempre pertinenti. Mi ha fatto estremamente piacere conoscere una persona così! Giovanni Levi, Tutor Logistica & Magazzino Contatti Nome Email Messaggio © Material CV. All right reserved by fabrizioterzi.eu
